verification.note: Read complete Marie von Clausewitz preface (30 June 1832), Notice (10 July 1827 and undated memorandum), Book I chapters VI–VII, Book II chapter III, and Book I chapter I sections 22–28. Supports editorial formation, uncertainty, friction, reacting opponents and variable relations of passion, chance and policy. Remaining chapters not read. Later editor’s Hague/great-war footnote is not Clausewitz; translation has not been collated against German or Howard/Paret.

wartradition.label: Strategic & military scholarship
wartradition.date_label: Earlier roots · Clausewitz’s On War 1832 · Delbrück’s volumes 1900–20
wartradition.description: Brings strategic reasoning, critical campaign scholarship and the editing of military texts into view. Clausewitz, Jomini, Delbrück, Mahan, Corbett and the translated Sun Tzu tradition pose different questions about judgment, evidence and the purposes of war. Professional education and academic inquiry overlap without being identical.
wartradition.representative_figures_and_works: Carl von Clausewitz, On War (1832); Hans Delbrück joins source criticism to analysis of warfare.

representative_people.context: Examines political purpose, passion, chance and friction in an unfinished, posthumously edited work. Strategic reasoning differs from empirical verification of particular campaigns.
representative_people.works: On War (1832); selected passages in Graham translation with later editorial apparatus

representative_people.context: Joins philological criticism to checks of practical possibility, using population evidence and documentary research. Explicitly acknowledges Ranke and Beloch; possible reconstructions are not automatically established events.
representative_people.works: Geschichte der Kriegskunst im Rahmen der politischen Geschichte, four volumes (1900–1920); first preface (1900)

representative_people.context: Proposes explaining sea power within general history and its social, political and economic surroundings. His naval-professional perspective and selected Europe/America scope are explicit.
representative_people.works: The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1660–1783 (1890), preface

representative_people.context: Treats naval operations within wider maritime coordination of armies, fleets and political purposes. Theory aids education and deliberation; this is a situated British imperial perspective.
representative_people.works: Some Principles of Maritime Strategy (1911), introduction

representative_people.context: Organizes posthumous publication and describes intellectual companionship and assistance from others. Her modest prefatory disclaimer does not make editorial work intellectually empty.
representative_people.works: Preface to On War, 30 June 1832

representative_people.context: Defends strategic principles while insisting that war also turns on morale, judgment and contingencies. His conclusion qualifies a wholly mechanical characterization.
representative_people.works: The Art of War, Mendell/Craighill translation (1862), conclusion

representative_people.context: Traditional attribution of a Chinese strategic text that prioritizes overcoming resistance and preserving forces over repeated destructive combat. Neither a fixed composition date nor a uniform Chinese tradition is asserted.
representative_people.works: The Art of War, Giles translation (1910), chapter III §§1–8

representative_people.context: Makes translation, paragraph arrangement and selective Chinese commentary part of the English text’s reception; his criticism of predecessors remains a contested editorial judgment.
representative_people.works: The Art of War (1910), translator’s preface and commentary

representative_people.context: Proposes and collaborates with Howard on a new Clausewitz translation. Strachan later assesses its modernization; translating does not simply transmit an unchanged meaning.
representative_people.works: With Michael Howard, On War (1976), translation; collaboration documented by Strachan

representative_people.context: Challenges Keegan’s culture/politics opposition while valuing The Face of Battle. Later web corrections are distinguished from the original polemic.
representative_people.works: “John Keegan and the Grand Tradition of Trashing Clausewitz” (1994)

representative_people.context: Collaborates with Paret on translating Clausewitz; readable modern vocabulary is also an object of later interpretive criticism.
representative_people.works: With Peter Paret, On War (1976), translation

representative_people.context: Questions Clausewitz through a cultural account of warfare, as represented in Bassford’s opposing reception. This is distinct from the combat-reconstruction method of his earlier book.
representative_people.works: A History of Warfare (1993), mediated by Bassford (1994)

representative_people.context: Delbrück explicitly credits demographic groundwork while correcting individual estimates. A named methodological resource, not acceptance of every army figure.
representative_people.works: Die Bevölkerung der griechisch-römischen Welt (1886), acknowledged in Delbrück’s 1900 preface

wartradition.scope_note: A selective teaching umbrella, weighted toward European and Anglophone scholarship, with a Chinese text and its mediated reception distinguished. Delbrück explicitly uses Ranke, Beloch and biographical research; these roots are not independent of every other historical tradition. Theory does not guarantee successful action. Marie’s editing and later translations are substantive mediation. Corbett writes for an imperial setting; neither that perspective nor Mahan’s national judgments is universalized. Bassford’s later online corrections are not assigned to his 1994 argument.

strands.title: Strategic principles, uncertainty and judgment
strands.focus: Clausewitz’s friction and variable tendencies and Jomini’s qualified rules frame different questions. Neither makes war wholly mechanical.
strands.works: On War (1832), selections; The Art of War (1862 translation), conclusion

strands.title: Editing and translating strategic texts
strands.focus: Marie’s posthumous work and Howard/Paret’s translation expose mediation and interpretive choices, rather than a single transparent text.

strands.title: Chinese strategic writing and its translation
strands.focus: Giles’s selection and commentary mediate the attributed Sun Tzu text. Overcoming resistance is not synonymous with winning repeated battles; wider Chinese traditions and textual dating need separate inquiry.
strands.works: The Art of War, Giles translation (1910), preface and III §§1–8

strands.title: Documents and practical possibility
strands.focus: Delbrück combines textual criticism with population and physical constraints, explicitly using Beloch and acknowledging Ranke. Possible alternatives remain distinct from proven events.

strands.title: Sea power and maritime coordination
strands.focus: Mahan proposes integrating sea power with general history; Corbett distinguishes naval operations from wider maritime strategy. This juxtaposition does not itself establish direct transmission.
strands.works: The Influence of Sea Power (1890), preface; Some Principles (1911), introduction

strands.title: Culture, politics and disputed reception
strands.focus: Keegan’s 1993 challenge and Bassford’s response are an exchange about interpreting Clausewitz. Bassford also values Keegan’s earlier work and acknowledges limits to strategic theory.
strands.works: A History of Warfare (1993), mediated; Bassford polemic (1994)

military.label: Military history
military.date_label: Earlier roots · Howard 1961 · Keegan 1976 · multiple paradigms
military.description: Studies campaigns and combat alongside institutions, societies, maritime power, gender and remembrance. Howard’s contextual reconstruction, Keegan’s critical study of battle and debates over military revolutions supply different methods and explanations. Source access, narrative framing and geographic scope shape their claims.
military.representative_figures_and_works: Distinct roots include Clausewitz, On War (1832), and Hans Delbrück; later examples: Michael Howard, John Keegan, and Joanna Bourke.

military.scope_note: A research field with overlapping objects, not one school or a progression that supersedes campaign history. Delbrück and strategic scholarship supply distinct resources; military historians also reinterpret and criticize them. Keegan’s restricted battle definition leaves much colonial and guerrilla experience outside its frame. European military-revolution debates extend to overseas encounters without representing the whole world’s military historiography. Bourke, Winter and Nell retain distinct questions about bodies, mourning and recognition. Scholarly collaboration, library work, editing and archival limits are part of the field’s production.

strands.title: Campaign reconstruction and documentary limits
strands.focus: Howard, Tuchman and Wedgwood connect decisions and circumstances through different narrative practices. Source access and explanatory selection remain objects of criticism.
strands.works: The Franco-Prussian War (1961); The Guns of August (1962); The Thirty Years War (1938)

strands.title: Combat experience and critical testimony
strands.focus: Keegan joins questions about bodies and behavior to criticism of memoirs, rhetoric and physical possibility. His selected battle frame does not represent all forms of war.
strands.works: The Face of Battle (1976), available excerpt

strands.title: War studies, research and teaching
strands.focus: Howard’s King’s work combines historical study with wider social, ethical and political inquiry. Library access, publishing and translation collaboration form part of the research setting.
strands.works: The Franco-Prussian War (1961); War in European History (1976)

strands.title: Naval history within wider explanation
strands.focus: Sea power and military/naval coordination widen a land-centered account. Mahan and Corbett state different purposes from a simple naval chronicle.

strands.title: Military revolutions: causes and chronology
strands.focus: Roberts, Parker, Rogers, Black and Lynn debate timing, mechanisms and evidence. Their accounts do not form one settled technological explanation.

strands.title: Finance, bargaining and geographic scope
strands.focus: Fiscal bargaining and overseas comparisons complicate a universal route from weapons to centralized power. The selected debate remains weighted toward European questions.

strands.title: Bodies, injury and masculinity
strands.focus: Bourke examines men’s bodies and wartime masculinity. This question differs from strategic success or adding women to a roster.

strands.title: Remembrance, mourning and recognition
strands.focus: Winter examines forms of mourning; Nell recovers Black military service from patriotic exclusion. These different projects broaden whose war is remembered.
strands.works: Sites of Memory, Sites of Mourning (1995); The Colored Patriots (1855)

strands.title: Cultural explanations and their critics
strands.focus: Keegan’s later account and Bassford’s opposition distinguish cultural interpretation from the earlier reconstruction of combat. Political purpose and culture need not be mutually exclusive.
strands.works: A History of Warfare (1993), mediated; Bassford (1994)

strands.title: Recruitment as labor and household strategy
strands.focus: Lucassen and Zürcher compare state recruitment options with recruits’ and households’ responses. Pay and freedom vary independently; different systems coexist. Their explicit use of Tilly connects fiscal capacity to recruitment and resistance.
